evidence.source: Shuowen Jiezi online transcription, entry 兩
evidence.field: text lines 6–8; Duan Yucai note lines 15–35
evidence.text: The received Shuowen entry defines 兩 as a weight of twenty-four zhu and analyzes it as 从一、㒳, with 㒳 meaning ‘divide evenly’ and also supplying sound. Duan Yucai likewise explains the weight as twice the weight of a Huangzhong measure, while treating 从一㒳 as associative; this is an early lexicographic analysis, not independent paleographic confirmation.
evidence.title: 說文解字「兩」 — Shuowen.org

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫, character entry 兩
evidence.text: The entry says bronze forms appear as 㒳, sometimes with an added top stroke; it presents the yoke/chariot-front explanation as a proposal attributed to 于省吾, and reports early bronze uses as a quantity word (‘two’) and a weight unit. It also notes a Warring States form with 羊 inside, interpreted as a sound marker. The page reports no oracle-bone forms for 兩, so its ancient examples are bronze, seal, and manuscript forms.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫 — 兩

evidence.source: 李運富, “兩字職用演變研究（一）,” 河南大學漢字文明研究中心
evidence.text: The study reports 㒳 as the initial form, attested in early Western Zhou bronze inscriptions such as 盝驹尊 and 卫盉; an upper stroke form 兩 appears by the Spring and Autumn period and gradually replaces 㒳, with 兩 dominant after the Han. It distinguishes the Shuowen/Duan account (㒳 for ‘two’, 兩 for the weight unit) from scholars who consider 㒳 and 兩 one graph. It reviews the yoke/chariot hypothesis and raises objections: the forms and early uses do not securely establish a noun meaning ‘vehicle’. It proposes, cautiously, a modified chariot-front form used as a dedicated measure for a pair of horses. This proposal remains a hypothesis, not a demonstrated original depiction.
evidence.title: “两”字职用演变研究（一）

evidence.source: 李運富, “兩字職用演變研究（一）,” 河南大學漢字文明研究中心
evidence.text: The article cites early Western Zhou examples using 兩/㒳 as a measure for horses: 《小臣宅簋》 (8.4201), “金車，馬兩”; 《小臣守簋盖》 (8.4179–4181), “宾马两”; a mid-Western Zhou example 《㒼簋》; and 《𤼈鼎》. It says this dedicated horse-pair measure declined by late Western Zhou. The article identifies its own publication as 2014 and later inclusion in a 2016 volume. These examples support early quantity/measure use, but their dating does not by itself prove the proposed graphic motivation.
evidence.title: “两”字职用演变研究（一）

evidence.source: 陳英傑, “戰國金文補證三則,” 復旦大學出土文獻與古文字研究中心
evidence.text: The article notes quantity uses in late Western Zhou bronze inscriptions (for example, ‘兩罍、兩壺’) and in Spring and Autumn material (‘兩壺、八鼎’), and traces related forms in Warring States manuscripts including 上博簡《亘先》 and 包山文書. It cautions that a continuity chain between earlier and later shapes is missing and that some later forms may have changed by graphic assimilation under the influence of 鬲. This is a specific gap in reconstructing the graphic pathway, not evidence that the readings are loans.
evidence.title: 陳英傑：戰國金文補證三則

evidence.source: Ministry of Education, Taiwan, Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants
evidence.text: The entry classifies 两 as a variant spelling of 兩 and records it in Song–Yuan vulgar character materials, quoting 《字學三正》 that 兩 was俗作两. It therefore predates contemporary simplified-character standardization as an attested variant; this particular source does not establish that this old variant was the direct historical basis of modern simplification.
evidence.title: [A00284-002] 两 (兩) — Ministry of Education Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants

evidence.source: Baxter and Sagart, “Baxter-Sagart Old Chinese reconstruction, version 1.1”
evidence.field: PDF lines 0–30 and search result for 丙
evidence.text: The authors’ 2014 reconstruction table specifies that its Old Chinese forms are reconstructed rather than directly observed, explains its notation and uncertainty markers, and describes its MC column as a transcription based on medieval sources such as Guangyun. Search-indexed table results give 丙 as Mandarin bǐng, Middle Chinese pjaengX, Old Chinese *praŋʔ, gloss ‘3d heavenly stem’. I could not retrieve the complete official PDF with the two target entries: the by-Mandarin PDF opened, but text search failed to locate entries; a second PDF attempt returned HTTP 502. The dossier’s *p.raŋʔ notation differs typographically from the search-indexed official *praŋʔ table notation; these should not be silently merged. No verified local Baxter–Sagart TSV row was available.
evidence.title: Baxter-Sagart Old Chinese reconstruction, version 1.1 (20 September 2014)

evidence.source: Baxter and Sagart, “Baxter-Sagart Old Chinese reconstruction, version 1.1”
evidence.field: data table search result and methodology note
evidence.text: The reconstructed 丙 *praŋʔ and the dossier’s 兩 *p.raŋʔ are similar in the Old Chinese transcription reported in the dossier and search-indexed official source, but a primary entry for 兩 could not be independently opened and compared. Thus the proposed 丙 phonetic analysis is plausible in sound terms but not verified here from the exact paired entries, and the graphic interpretation of the two forms remains a separate question. Do not treat this reconstructed comparison as evidence for the meaning or name of a depicted chariot part.
evidence.title: Baxter-Sagart Old Chinese reconstruction, version 1.1 (20 September 2014)

gaps: No image was visually inspected, and the Sinica dynamic evolution page did not expose its glyph records in extracted text. Graphic descriptions above rely on inspected textual scholarly/dictionary analyses.

The chariot-yoke hypothesis is attributed to 于省吾 and repeated in the CUHK dictionary, but the inspected study disputes the claim that the original graph simply depicts a vehicle and explicitly notes lack of secure vehicle-noun attestations. The exact original depicted object remains unresolved.

A proposal that the graph derived from a chariot front and represented one or two horses is explicitly hypothetical. The reconstructed sound of 丙 does not establish a depicted implement’s original name or prove a whole-graph loan; no whole-graph loan claim is adopted.

The dossier’s suggestion of two 丙 forms joined graphically is not confirmed by the primary material inspected. It may conflate a modern component parse with a disputed historical analysis. The character’s graphic component analysis should remain unsettled.

The exact paired Baxter–Sagart entries for 丙 and 兩 could not be checked in the official PDF output; no local baxtersagart.tsv exists in this checkout. The dossier’s notation *p.raŋʔ and the official indexed *praŋʔ display differ; retain system-specific spellings and avoid asserting an exact phonetic reconstruction from this evidence.
The checked repository has only the HSK1 reading extract, which covers neither character nor 丙. No local kMandarin rows were available for these readings.

Per-character official Unicode GetUnihanData URLs were attempted for U+4E24, U+5169 and U+4E19 and failed to load. Modern kMandarin values are reported only from secondary transcriptions; UAX #38 establishes the data-property framework but not those exact records.

The inspected early bronze citations establish pair/measure and weight uses by Western Zhou, but the available pages do not establish a secure absolute first attestation for the abstract numeral ‘two’, nor a dated semantic chain from horse-pair measure to all later senses. Do not infer chronology from a dictionary gloss list.
No inspected source establishes Japanese character origin; Japanese readings in the dossier are later readings and not evidence of Japanese-created formation.
No rights or bulk-reuse grant for CUHK, Sinica, MOE, or article content was verified. A mirror extract is not recommended; cite concise character-specific paraphrases.
